title: Commonly confused pairs
objectives: Explain 15 commonly confused pairs in one line each, with a rupee example.
Test a partner on any pair in under 30 seconds.
body_md:
These are the mix-ups that cause the most client complaints and wrong decisions. NAV is calculated once a day from holdings; a share price changes every second — and a low NAV is not “cheap”. Absolute return ignores time; CAGR annualises a lump sum; XIRR annualises money in or out on different dates. Growth reinvests; IDCW pays out of your own money. Exit load is a fee; lock-in blocks exit. Volatility is a temporary swing; a loss becomes real only when you sell or a borrower defaults.

| Often confused | The difference in one line |
| --- | --- |
| NAV vs share price | NAV is calculated once a day from holdings; a share price changes every second on the exchange. A low NAV is not "cheap" |
| Absolute return vs CAGR | 100% over 5 years is about 14.9% a year, not 20% |
| CAGR vs XIRR | CAGR for one lump sum; XIRR when money goes in or out on different dates (SIPs) |
| Direct vs regular plan | Same portfolio and manager; regular includes distributor commission for advice and service |
| Growth vs IDCW | Growth reinvests; IDCW pays out of your own money and the NAV falls by the payout. It is not extra income |
| Exit load vs lock-in | Exit load: you can leave but pay a fee. Lock-in: you cannot leave at all |
| TER vs exit load | TER is a yearly running cost in the NAV; exit load is a one-time fee only on early exit |
| SIP vs STP | SIP moves money from your bank; STP moves money from one fund to another |
| SWP vs IDCW | SWP: you choose a fixed amount; IDCW: the fund decides if and how much to pay |
| Risk tolerance vs risk capacity | Tolerance: how much fall you can stomach. Capacity: how much fall your finances can afford |
| Volatility vs loss | Volatility is a temporary swing; a loss becomes real only when you sell or when a borrower defaults |
| Diversification vs many funds | Five funds holding the same stocks is not diversification |
| Nominal vs real return | Real return is what's left after inflation |
| YTM vs guaranteed return | YTM is today's indicative yield; debt fund returns are not guaranteed |
| Riskometer vs suitability | The riskometer labels the fund; suitability matches the fund to the client |

> **Investor takeaway:** Ask a new joiner to explain each pair to a partner in under 30 seconds, using a rupee example.
example: ₹1 lakh → ₹2 lakh in 5 years is 100% absolute, about 14.9% CAGR — not 20% a year.
say: SWP: you choose the amount. IDCW: the fund decides.
Five funds holding the same stocks is not diversification.
never: A low NAV fund is cheap.
